title: Soft-boundary token merge controller — exploratory sketch
abstract: Sketch of an alternative continuous batching controller that uses soft boundaries for token aggregation and a per-token credit system to balance request-level latency with token-level packing efficiency. Focuses on kernel-friendly batch blending and interactions with KV cache handoff. Experimental plan and open questions included.
body:
Goal and context:
This doc is exploratory — not a polished spec. I want to capture a different approach to continuous batching that: (a) avoids hard request boundaries, (b) enables more consistent kernel work shapes for long/short requests, and (c) preserves fairness across tenants and SLA classes.

Motivation / problem statements we repeatedly see:
- Token-level batching gives best throughput but can starve short-latency requests (esp tail latency).
- Request-level batching preserves request boundaries and SLAs but leaves tokens on the table (lower utilization).
- Kernel performance is sensitive to sequence length distribution and KV cache access patterns; mixing widely different shapes in one microbatch can regress throughput on certain kernels.
- Existing continuous coalescers either use sticky windows or strict cutoffs; these introduce discontinuities and complicate rollouts.

High-level idea: soft-boundary token merge controller
- Controller treats each incoming request as a chain of token segments (logical chunks). Instead of locking tokens to a request boundary, tokens are assigned a soft "merge credit" that represents how aggressively they may be merged with other requests in the current microbatch.
- Merge credits decay over time; requests that wait longer gain extra credits (helps fairness).
- A per-GPU microbatch builder observes tokens in the ready queue and selects a blend that optimizes an objective: weighted combination of kernel-cost estimate, expected latency impact, and fairness penalty.

Core components:
1) Segmentizer: on request arrival, split request into segments using heuristic (prefix length / prompt boundary / sampling of token-likelihood peaks). Segments provide atomic units for merging (not individual tokens).
2) Credit ledger: small per-request ledger with two numbers: current_credits and last_updated_ts. Credits start low, increment slowly (or start medium if request has high SLA) and increase with waiting time. Credits consumed when segment is merged into a microbatch.
3) BatchBlender: optimization loop that considers candidate segments and greedily selects combination to reach a target token budget for the microbatch while minimizing kernel heterogeneity cost. Kernel heterogeneity cost is estimated by computing a simple variance score over segment sequence lengths plus a penalty when some segments require different quantization/kernel paths.
4) KernelHinting: segments carry lightweight hints (seq_len_estimate, kv_hotness_estimate, quant_profile_tag) derived from model metadata and prior runs; BatchBlender uses these to avoid mixing segments that will trigger slow kernels together.
5) KV Handoff contract: when segments from multiple requests share an activation KV state (e.g., continuation of chat), we introduce a KV affinity flag to keep segments of the same request contiguous within the same microbatch or ensure KV prefetch is scheduled. The flag reduces merging credits for those segments unless explicit cache prefetch is triggered.

Fairness and SLA rules (sketch):
- Credit weighting: credits are multiplied by SLA_weight; e.g., interactive requests get 1.5x accrual rate, background jobs 0.6x.
- Max wait bound: every request has a soft max-wait where credits jump to a high priority to bound tail latency. This is configurable per-route.
- Proportional merge cap: when building a microbatch, ensure no single tenant/request contributes >X% of tokens unless util < threshold. This prevents hogging.
- Drift correction: keep an exponentially weighted moving average of per-request latency; if a request class is seeing widening tail, temporarily bias BatchBlender to prioritize that class.

Kernel-aware batch shaping heuristics:
- Prefer grouping segments with similar seq_len_estimate modulo a small window to reduce kernel padding overhead.
- Penalize combining segments where quant_profile_tag differs (e.g. 4-bit vs 8-bit paths) unless batch will be split across kernel lanes and still be beneficial.
- If KV hotness_estimate is high, prefer to put those segments at head of microbatch to maximize cache warmup.

KV cache interactions:
- Prefetch policy: when BatchBlender considers merging a segment that requires KV state not present locally, it can: (a) skip merging that segment, (b) include it only if a background prefetch ticket is issued and prefetch completes within X ms, or (c) accept higher latency for that segment and annotate metrics.
- Handoff semantics: for private/enterprise deployments with strict data isolation, we keep KV-affinity conservative (favor request-level contiguity). For hosted mode we can be more aggressive.
- Consistency note: segments that depend on previous hidden state must enforce logical order; Segmentizer marks them as ordered and those segments must either be kept contiguous or have deterministic state replay.

Simulation plan / metrics to collect:
- Offline replay harness: run 24h production trace through a simulator that implements the credit accrual and BatchBlender objective. Outputs: average tokens-per-batch, average microbatch kernel shape variance, 95/99 latency per route, fairness index (Jain's index across tenants), wasted tokens due to padding.
- Kernel-level microbench: feed candidate blended batches into kernel perf microbench to validate the estimated kernel heterogeneity cost vs actual.
- A/B rollout plan: start in canary region with 5% traffic, expose per-request trace IDs and additional tracing for KV prefetch events. Monitor tail latencies and error rates for 1 week before increasing traffic.

Open questions / risks:
- Credit tuning complexity: many knobs (accrual rate, SLA multipliers, max-wait) — risk of misconfiguration. Need adaptive autotune or simple defaults.
- Kernel hint accuracy: if hints are noisy, BatchBlender may make suboptimal groupings. Consider lightweight online calibration that updates seq_len_estimate distribution per model.
- Complexity vs maintainability: adding Segmentizer, credits, KV pref etc increases code surface area. Is the throughput win worth it compared to simpler windowing schemes?
- Multi-GPU microbatch coordination: when batching across GPUs (for large tokens), coordinating credits and fairness is trickier. Option: do per-GPU local selection with occasional global adjustments via a coordinator tick. Need experiments.

Short-term deliverables (next 8 weeks):
- Week 1–2: implement a toy simulator and Segmentizer with synthetic traces. Validate simple heuristics.
- Week 3–4: integrate kernel hinting and run microbench against common kernel footprints.
- Week 5–6: run replay on 2 days of production trace, iterate on credit accrual parameters.
- Week 7–8: build a canary agent for 5% traffic with extensive telemetry and a kill-switch.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Decide on default segment size heuristic: fixed 16-token segments vs prompt-aware breakpoints. (bookmark: discussion in #serving-runtime on 2024-10-11)
- Add unit tests for credit ledger under concurrent segment arrivals.
- Design data model for KernelHinting tags — must be compact (one byte tag preferred) to avoid storage blowup.
- Write short RFC for ops describing new metrics (Jain fairness, kernel heterogeneity score).

Experimental knobs to expose in Console:
- accrual_rate, sla_multiplier_map, max_wait_ms, token_budget_target, max_tokens_per_request_percent, kernel_homogeneity_bias.

Rough pseudocode (very high level):
- on_request(req): segs = segmentize(req); for seg in segs: credit_ledger[req.id]+=init_credit; enqueue(seg)
- on_schedule_tick(): candidates = dequeue_ready_segments(); while token_budget not reached: pick seg that maximizes score = credits*weight - kernel_penalty - latency_penalty; mark seg selected; consume credits; build microbatch; dispatch

Unresolved config defaults (proposals):
- default accrual_rate: 1 credit / 20ms for interactive; 1 credit / 50ms for background
- initial credit: interactive 2, background 0.5
- token_budget_target: 2048 tokens per microbatch (tunable)

Appendix: brief comparison vs examples in repo (why different)
- Unlike pure token-level continuous coalescers, this approach keeps an explicit credit-driven fairness ledger to guarantee bounded tail latency.
- Unlike strict request-aware windows, it supports safe mixing of segments when kernel and KV hints align, improving utilization.

Links and references:
- internal threads: slack://thread/serving-runtime/ABC123
- related tickets: JIRA-RT-1119 (kv-prefetch), JIRA-RT-1205 (kernel-hint-tags)

Last quick thought: keep the implementation incremental. Start with segmentizer + credit ledger + simple greedy BatchBlender. If we see good results, we can add more sophisticated global optimization and autotune.

End of sketch.
